177.t: Glass-disc home recording with Burbank, Talbot and Lester Lewis
177.s: A four-piece home recording made during the war, with glass blanks, in the Orleans Street project; Lewis's piano and where Talbot's widow might live.
177.q: Lewis the piano player? Yes. Well, he was a quite nice Dixieland piano player. And he gave it up. He stopped playing. But he was a very good piano player.

243.t: Records made, and the Navy radio shows
243.s: He discusses records with Fats Pichon, an unreleased Southland session with Jeanette, Jim Robinson and George Lewis, and Friday radio shows at the Naval Air Station.
243.q: Those records I told you about made with Jeanette and Jim Robinson, George Lewis, Paul Barberin. But I don't think those records were ever released. I don't know what happened to them. I know we made them. We went up there one day and we cut about six sides or something. Four either six sides. Had…

241.t: Whether the country bands or he recorded
241.s: No recordings were made by the country bands, and he had no chance to record when he first moved to the city.
241.ch: Family, records and the Moulin Rouge years
241.q: Uh huh, yeah, yeah. You never saw anybody take a machine around? No, I ain't never seen nobody. Cause most of all the bands that they had, that was Marshall Lawrence and their band they had, and all bands they had that. And uh, so we never did, they never did record no uh, no record to my name.

253.t: Mutt Carey recordings and the Red Book
253.s: Hall met Mutt Carey in New York for their recordings, including African Misk; the group discusses reissues and the Red Books.
253.q: I met, I met Mud, the first time I met Mud was in New York. And that was the time that we made this recording. I heard about him because he was in California because he came to New York for a while.

1023.t: Recording with Sharkey in New Orleans at the Roosevelt Hotel
1023.s: He recorded a session with Sharkey locally at the Roosevelt Hotel, supervised by the Decca founder, and collectors still seek those records.
1023.q: Well, that was done down here. We made a record down here. And one side of that was Yes She Does, No She Don't, and I forget the Everybody Lows My Baby or something like that was on the other side. Yeah, I remember that. We made that in the Roosevelt Hotel. And strangely enough, the guy who founded…

763.t: Guitar duet with Rappolo on the NORK Gennett session
763.s: He recalls the Indianapolis recording where he and Rappolo played guitar duets, Carol Pierce's Marguerite, and that the duet was never released.
763.q: Yeah, when we made that recording in Indianapolis, at the time, you know, with the big band, that we, with New Orleans, Harlem Kings, we, rap and I played a duet with two guitars. He played the blues and I made the accompaniments, you know, behind him. But we made the recording, but I never heard…

734.t: Playing with Percy Humphrey and the Dumaine records
734.s: Fraternity and country club jobs with Percy Humphrey; Dumaine records on Rampart Street.
734.q: Yeah, yeah. We made it somewhere down on Rampart Street. On Rampart Street. Yeah. And Pretty Audrey, I know that was one of the songs, Pretty Audrey. Yes. And uh, Franklin Street Blues. But I didn't play it on that record. That girl woman sing on that record. That woman sing on that record. That…

46.t: Black Patti and the Melrose recording session
46.s: He recalls recording Boar Hog Blues and Squeeze Me for Black Patti, and a Melrose session that ended when he refused to change the trombone note.
46.q: Yeah. Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Yeah. No, he was a, no, wait a minute, I can't think of the, but we cut, I cut, I think, four, four numbers, before, I made, I recorded, the boy called blues, and squeezed me. Bull Hog on one side and squeezed me is on the other.

121.t: Bob Robin's River City Records and the Baton Rouge session
121.s: Ridgley recalls River City sides recorded in Baton Rouge with Bob Robin, a guitarist's playing, and unreleased tracks and a good-selling record.
121.q: River City. Bob Robin. Okay. Now, what year that could have been around? 1960? It's probably like 60s. Not very late. About 67, 60, 68, 69, somewhere around there. Okay. Yeah, because I was thinking, I remember when I was in that nightclub. And I was supposed to be running a nightclub. But anyway,…

779.t: Leon Rappolo and recording at the Bucktown roadhouse
779.s: His sister question turns into Bucktown band, declined free record, and Johnny's clarinet.
779.ch: Stories of players and the sister
779.q: Yeah, Bernie, no. You see, the first time when I was working out of the Bugtown, Leon Rapport was playing out there, and George E. Brunus, Joe Gowler was playing piano, myself. We used to have corner players. We never had any corner players. We used to have corner players just come in and sit in,…

306.t: The Kid Rena recording and Hayward Brown
306.s: Rene and Allen discuss how to find Rena's Delta Jazz Band record and who issued it, and a detour about a television sportscaster.
306.q: I don't know if you can go to Ikes for King René's Delta Giant Band. The Giant Band, you can get it under that name. They got the history and everything. I don't know the record to a fella. I had it here for quite a while. And a fella wanted so bad, so I don't know if I can take it. I ain't gonna…

309.t: Recordings with Frank Arnold and the unconcerned family attitude
309.s: He made records with Frank Arnold with Smitty and Anderson, never heard them, and says the family just did its own thing.
309.ch: Records and playing in New Orleans
309.q: Yeah. I made several records with him. Mm-hmm. But I don't know what happened. He and the union had some kind of a little misunderstanding, and he never did get the records or something. He never did get the recordings.

966.s: Davis recalls three usable takes on son Cole's composition, the soloists Troy Roberts and Mike Rodriguez, and drummer Jared Schonig playing while sick.
966.ch: Open City and the economics of records
966.q: I do actually. Thank you for mentioning that track. I’m super fond of it and it was actually a composition/arrangement by my son, Cole Davis, who is an outstanding bass player and writer as well. And that was three takes. We did three takes on that. And all three of them were usable. In fact…

451.t: The live Bourbon Street record in Toronto
451.s: Toronto trio recorded by Don Thompson.
451.q: We played at this club in Toronto. Oh, it was funny. I had gone up there a few times to work. Tell me the name of the club ‘cause it’s on…

99.t: Friendship with Ferguson, reading, and Gennett records at Richmond, Indiana
99.s: Pillars reads in the library, learns golf from Ferguson, and the band records 'Clementine' and 'I Found a New Baby' for Gennett.
99.q: By all means. And that's the way it was. We played all through that territory and Mr. Ferguson became one of my best friends, he took me out -- the first golf ball I ever hit in my life, he taught me how to hold a club. C. Ferguson, A very fine person and a very smart business man.

412.t: The Child's disc recordings and the Jazz Record reissues
412.s: Joe Grasso kept a disc recorder by his drums and made recordings of the band. Hodes says these came out on the Jazz Record label and may be reissued by George Buck.
412.q: We put that out eventually -- well, here's what happened. We did not record for a label. Joe Grasso had a disc recorder of some sort. One of those ancient ones. And he brought that in one night and kept it by his drums. And while he was playing drums, he would operate this thing. And you know how…

388.t: Recording with Edmund Hall and Walter Page for Decca
388.s: Edmund Hall asks Leeman to record at Decca with Ralph Sutton and Walter Page, and Leeman later fails to recognize his own brushes on playback.
388.q: Hall, who was wonderful. He asked me to do a couple of recordings with him, and we went up to Decca and recorded -- "Big 'n' a" with him, we Ralph Sutton was on piano, and he took Walter Page up, and we made one or two recordings or albums -- I forget which; there was a transition then from 78's…

7.t: The lost Stormy Weather record with Benny Carter and Jacquet
7.s: He recalls a California recording with Benny Carter, Illinois Jacquet and Hilton Jefferson that none of them has, and noisy old records.
7.ch: After Cab: Don Redman, teaching and records
7.q: And that's how I found out how them great... I learned something about writing for bass from that guy, that arranger out there -- I can't think of his name now. That's the time when Benny Carter came out, and we made a recording of...
